h: The Ramlila crowd, and a mould of power that is cracking
dek: Veteran journalist Anand K. Sahay says the 1 November rally broke the mould in which the Modi government never made room for dissent; the real test now is the Uttar Pradesh election.
ank: people whose vote was taken away, says the writer
elections in UP and other states
body: Anand K. Sahay calls himself an old newsman, and in this piece his memory is his argument. He says the crowd seen on 1 November at Ramlila Maidan, and on the roads from there to Connaught Place, has made the government uneasy. Ministers are calling it a 'flop show', but the writer says live footage and drone pictures prove that claim false. Amit Shah linked the rally's date to the anniversary of Indira Gandhi's assassination and the anti-Sikh riots that followed, which the writer sees as petty politics.

In Sahay's view this crowd was unmatched on this ground in the last half century. He witnessed Jayaprakash Narayan's rally in February 1977, a few weeks after which the Janata Party defeated the Congress. He says even that rally was not this big, and its crowd did not spill onto the roads. Rahul Gandhi was at the centre; student leader Neha Bora, who had also been at the 'people's impeachment' of the Chief Election Commissioner the evening before, fired up the young in particular.

The writer sees this as a link in a chain that began in July. Then, protests by the 'Cockroach' movement, Left student groups and Congress-linked groups forced the Union education minister to quit. He says that in the RSS-BJP tradition ministers do not bow to protest, so that resignation was the first crack in a carefully built image of strength, and Ramlila split it wide open.

Sahay also recalls the 2024 election, when the BJP fell short of a majority, and says that instead of following a High Court direction to hand over videos of the polling, the government changed the rules themselves at the Commission's request. The revelations about SIR have made the picture murkier. According to the writer, technically 13 crore people lost their vote under Gyanesh Kumar's watch, though people believe the order came from above.

In the end he puts questions to both sides. How will the government face angry, organised voters over the next three months, especially in Uttar Pradesh? And can the Opposition turn this energy into state-by-state movements and electoral alliances? The Chief Election Commissioner has been silent for weeks, and the writer says that for now there are more questions than answers.
nazar: Sahay's piece is full of hope, but its most honest point comes at the end: a crowd is not politics by itself. The comparison with 1977 will hold only if Ramlila's energy reaches the booths, the appeals and the return of cut names. For the 13 crore people whose names are at stake, what matters more than a picture of the rally is whether they get to vote in February.
sawal: With the drone pictures out, what exactly is the 'flop show'?
ref: The February 1977 rally
Jayaprakash Narayan's meeting at Ramlila Maidan after the Emergency, a few weeks after which the Janata Party came to power.
The Deserted Village
Oliver Goldsmith's 1770 poem, one line of which mocks a man who keeps arguing even after he has lost; the writer applies it to the government.

h: Names do not return to the roll from a rally stage
dek: In an Amar Ujala column, Vinod Pathak asks the Opposition for evidence on SIR instead of slogans, and asks the Commission for accountability too.
body: Vinod Pathak sees the Special Intensive Revision of the voter rolls, or SIR, not as some unusual political move but as a basic condition for a clean election. He says the Congress and its allies are behaving as though the roll were being checked for the first time. Referring to the 1 November rally at Ramlila Maidan, he notes that the organisers claimed about ten lakh people, while Delhi Police estimated fifty thousand.

The writer says the real question is what happened on the ground: how many wrongful deletions were proved, how many complaints were filed, how many were heard and how many names were added back. His argument is that a person's vote is saved not by announcements from a stage but by identification at the booth and evidence placed before the Commission.

He gives two examples. In Kerala, at a review meeting in March, most parties including the Congress praised the calm conduct of SIR. In Karnataka, 99.76 lakh names were removed out of about 5.54 crore voters, a large share of them people who had moved away for good, were absent, had died or were entered twice; of the 43.82 lakh who got notices, 43.2 lakh stayed on the roll. Citing minister Satish Jarkiholi's statement and his later clarification, he asks whether the objection is to the idea of SIR or to the way it was carried out.

Pathak reminds us that the last big revision took place between 2002 and 2004, that Article 324 gives the Commission the power, and that on 27 May 2026 the Supreme Court held the process valid, though it stressed transparency and safeguards. But he does not let the Commission off either: the reason for every cut name should be made public, hearings should be meaningful, appeals should be settled on time and the figures should be checked independently.

In the end he advises the Opposition that questioning institutions after every defeat should not become its whole programme; it should also put forward real alternatives on jobs, prices and farmers' incomes.
nazar: This column is a voice that disagrees with the movement, and that is exactly why it is worth reading. The demand for evidence and booth-level work is fair. The trouble is that the writer puts the burden on the side that does not have the data. The reason for every cut name, a machine-readable roll, the record of hearings: all of this is with the Commission, not the Opposition. Until the Commission makes it public, taking to the streets is the only way left for this demand to be heard.
Karnataka's own figures show that almost one voter in five lost their name. If all of it was correct, why should the Commission fear transparency?
sawal: Who should prove a deletion: the voter, or the office that deleted the name?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission process in which the voter roll is rebuilt from scratch through door-to-door checks, and dead, shifted or duplicate names are removed.
Form 7
The application to object to a name on the voter roll and have it removed. The Opposition alleges it was used in bulk to get the names of legitimate voters cut.

h: Who holds the key to the voter roll, the Commission or a company?
dek: Journalist S. Raghotham asks why TCS, which built the software that cut more than 13 crore names, should not answer to the public.
body: Bengaluru journalist and researcher S. Raghotham makes a simple argument: if a private company's software overrides the decisions of officers who hold legal authority, and crores of citizens are pushed off the roll, that company must be held accountable. TCS built the Election Commission's ERONet and ECINet portals, as the company's own annual report admits.

Under the law, correcting the roll is the job of the local Electoral Registration Officer, so that no single office controls the country's voters. The writer says these portals pulled that power to the centre. He gives the example of Goa: officers found 97 people eligible, the Supreme Court told them to accept this, but the software had no way to record that decision. The state IT agency wrote eight times in six days, got no reply, and the final roll was printed without these 97.

In the 'logical discrepancy' check, people were marked suspect over things like a small age gap between parent and child, siblings born less than nine months apart, or the spelling of a name. Even 92-year-old Amartya Sen got a notice. In Uttar Pradesh, 98.5 per cent of 87,127 Form-7 objections gave no reason, and some officers said that even when they refused after a hearing, the system generated a deletion form using their digital signature.

The writer also sets out the donations from the Tata group's electoral trust to the BJP: in 2024-25, 757.6 crore of 915 crore went to the BJP. He says plainly that this does not prove any link between donations and contracts. He wants answers to six questions, the most important being: who set the limits of the family tree, and will TCS open its logs to an independent audit?
nazar: This piece moves the debate away from Gyanesh Kumar as a person and towards the machine, and that is its strength. Officers may change, but if software decides who is a citizen, accountability gets lost in some file. Migrant workers, poor women and people whose names are spelt in different ways are the first to be caught in such checks. The code behind the roll should be open to public scrutiny.
sawal: Who will cross-examine the software that cut the name?
ref: ERONet / ECINet
The Election Commission's digital portals through which names are added to, changed in and removed from the voter roll.
Progressive Electoral Trust
An electoral trust linked to the Tata group, through which companies donate to political parties.

h: When cut names outnumber the winning margin
dek: CPI(M) general secretary M.A. Baby says Bengal's figures and the dissent inside the Commission show that Gyanesh Kumar has to go.
body: CPI(M) general secretary M.A. Baby begins with the memory of T.N. Seshan: for all his faults, the Commission looked impartial in that era. He says the opposite happened after Gyanesh Kumar arrived: living, genuine voters were pushed off the roll, and even Bharat Ratna C.N.R. Rao and actor Prakash Raj had to make rounds of offices to get their vote back.

The piece rests on an Indian Express investigation which found that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected at least 14 times in ten months to orders issued in the Commission's name without their knowledge. One of these was adding a question about grandparents' names to Form-6, which Sandhu called illegal in writing. In Bengal 38 lakh appeals are pending, of which 16.10 lakh were filed by the Commission itself to get names cut.

Bengal's figures are the heaviest part of the piece. About 91 lakh names, or nearly 12 per cent of voters, were removed in SIR. In 49 seats, the names cut after hearings alone were more than the winning margin. Rajarhat New Town was decided by 316 votes, while 24,132 names had been cut. The writer accepts that this does not prove whom the excluded people would have voted for, but says that when those shut out outnumber the margin of victory, democracy cannot rest easy.

Baby also points to how commissioners are appointed. In March 2023 a Constitution bench said a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice should choose them. The government passed a law that put its own minister in place of the Chief Justice. He has four demands: remove Gyanesh Kumar and prosecute him, halt SIR, restore all eligible names, and set up a transparent selection system.
nazar: This is a party leader's piece and its language is just that, but its numbers speak louder than any slogan. A 316-vote win next to 24 thousand cut names questions every bit of trust an election stands on. The real lesson lies in the appointment law: as long as the government has a majority at the table that picks the umpire, the problem will not go away when one officer does.
sawal: A 316-vote win, 24 thousand names cut: whose result is it?
ref: Anoop Baranwal judgment
The 2023 ruling of a Supreme Court Constitution bench that said the Chief Justice should be part of the panel choosing Election Commissioners.
Article 324
The part of the Constitution that gives the Election Commission charge of conducting and overseeing elections.

h: A letter to a friend: the Commission is not the ruling party's executioner
dek: Former Kerala Chief Electoral Officer Teeka Ram Meena asks his batchmate Gyanesh Kumar for both a resignation and an account.
body: The voice in K.A. Shaji's piece is that of Teeka Ram Meena, an IAS officer of the 1988 batch in the Kerala cadre, exactly like Gyanesh Kumar. Meena calls him a sharp officer and a good friend, but says friendship is not bigger than constitutional duty. His worry goes beyond SIR: is the Commission independent of the government of the day?

Meena says that as Kerala's Chief Electoral Officer he never checked whether someone was in power or in opposition before acting on a breach of the code of conduct. In November last year he sent Kumar a list of complaints and got no reply. He then wrote to the other two commissioners, asking them to go by the rules and challenge wrong decisions. He feels that after this they began to question some of Kumar's decisions. The gist of his words is that the Commission is a body of three members, not one person.

Meena is not against cleaning up the rolls; he accepts that rolls contain fake names, dead people and people who have moved elsewhere. His objection is to the method and the timing: why such a huge exercise on the eve of elections, and why were parties and the public not involved? He calls the changes to Form-6 illegal, and says that if voters are afraid, something is wrong somewhere.

On the question of pressure he is careful. He has a 'deep suspicion' that Kumar was working under pressure, but accepts that he cannot prove it. On former Kerala chief secretary Jiji Thomson's allegation that Kumar had advised him to take a BJP ticket, Meena says a single allegation proves nothing, but it must be denied. He wants Kumar to resign, explain his decisions, and have the decisions of past years investigated.
nazar: Meena's voice carries weight because it comes from inside the same bureaucracy whose retired officers are mostly silent, out of fear of investigation, as Meena himself says. When a batchmate says the Commission cannot become the ruling party's executioner, that is not an Opposition slogan but unease from inside the institution. The lesson for the movement is that bringing such witnesses onto the stage will do more than slogans.
sawal: Is not answering a batchmate's letter an answer in itself?
ref: Chief Electoral Officer
The Election Commission's officer in each state, who looks after the voter roll and the running of elections there.
Model Code of Conduct
Rules for how parties and governments must behave during elections, which the Commission has to enforce.

h: Siasat's editorial: at Ramlila Maidan, the people's anger spoke
dek: Hyderabad's Urdu paper Siasat says the Ramlila rally was not a show of strength by any one party but the start of a fight for the right to vote.
body: In its editorial, Siasat calls the INDIA alliance rally of 1 November a clear example of public anger. The paper puts the crowd at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, gathered against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and SIR, in the lakhs, and says the gathering sent a message to both the government and the Election Commission that people will not quietly put up with 'vote theft'.

In the paper's view, vote theft is no longer just an allegation; it is being seen as a planned conspiracy meant to strip crores of citizens of their right to vote. The editorial says the attacks on the rally by BJP leaders are really panic, because the government fears this movement could spread across the country.

The most important part of the editorial is about who was at the rally. The paper says the poor, people whose names are missing from the roll, students, young people, farmers, lawyers, social workers, civil society and artists were all there. On this basis it calls it a fight of the people, not of parties: to protect democracy, the Constitution and civil rights, and against crores of Indians being made second-class citizens.

The paper also notes that although the rally was in Delhi, people came from almost every state. It says these were ordinary citizens angry at tampering with voter rolls and the disregard of election rules. The editorial hopes this public awareness will outweigh the government's tactics, that the campaign will reach every corner of the country, and that it may even mark the start of the ruling party's decline.
nazar: Siasat's editorial voices the unease of the community that is the first to be viewed with suspicion in the 'infiltrator' debate. For them a cut name is not just an election figure but a blow to the feeling of being a citizen, and that is why the phrase 'second-class citizens' weighs so heavily.

But along with the passion there is a gap: the editorial cites no hard figures, no region, no recorded case. If the movement is to last, it must gather an account of every cut name along with the crowds.
sawal: How can a rally crowd be turned into strength at the booth?
ref: Siasat
An Urdu daily published from Hyderabad since 1949, with strong influence among Muslim readers in South India.
Ramlila Maidan
A historic ground in Delhi where JP held a meeting in 1975 and the Anna movement took place in 2011; the INDIA alliance rally was held here on 1 November 2026.

h: A BJP leader's advice: skip the rallies, get the forms filled
dek: Meenakashi Lekhi says the claim that '13 crore names were cut' is misleading, and the Opposition should work at the booths instead of on the streets.
body: The day after the Ramlila rally, BJP leader and lawyer Meenakashi Lekhi wrote a defence of SIR, which she calls her personal opinion. She sees protest as a democratic right, but says allegations and facts must be separated and the matter will be settled through legal means. Her basis is Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which gives the Commission the power to keep the roll updated and to carry out a special revision after recording its reasons.

Giving the example of her old New Delhi constituency, she says the names of dead people and those who had moved elsewhere stayed on the roll there, and one driver was a voter in both Delhi and Bihar. She recalls that intensive revisions took place many times from 1952 to 2004, and also that before voter ID cards people used to cast votes in other people's names, and nobody complained of vote theft then.

The central claim of the piece is about the 13 crore figure. Lekhi says about 13.39 crore voters were put in the absent, shifted, dead or duplicate column of the draft roll; this is not the final deletion, and the final roll is made only after claims and objections. She accepts that no system is perfect, and mentions the case of the 97 voters in Goa. Without citing a source, she also alleges that foreigners' names were added in Delhi, Jammu and Telangana.

On EVMs she lists a long run of elections, including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Punjab and Karnataka, that Opposition parties won, and says a bad workman blames his tools. Her advice is that Rahul Gandhi and his allies should give up reels and sit-ins and get people to fill Forms 6, 7 and 8.
nazar: Lekhi's piece is the clearest sample of the ruling side's argument, and so it is worth reading. But her advice contradicts itself: the very Form-6 she wants people to fill has been changed in a way that two of the Commission's commissioners have called illegal. Saying 'draft deletions are not final' is comforting only when appeals are heard on time; in Bengal most appeals were still hanging when the election came. Putting the burden on the citizen and saying 'work at the booth' dodges the real question.
sawal: Cutting names is the Commission's job, and restoring them the Opposition's?
ref: Forms 6, 7 and 8
Form-6 is for adding a new name, Form-7 for removing a name or objecting to one, and Form-8 for changing an address or other details.
ASDD
The grouping of voters as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, on the basis of which names were removed from the draft roll in SIR.

h: US midterms: the Left showed that it can win
dek: Jacobin's Branko Marcetic says the success of socialist and pro-people candidates in the Democrats' big win has broken the fear that left policies lose votes.
body: In the 3 November midterm elections, the Democratic Party flipped both houses and won its biggest congressional majority since Obama's victory in 2008. People were angry about prices and about Trump, though they were not happy with the Democratic Party either. Even so, the win reached deep Republican areas like Texas, which nobody had expected.

The writer's real argument is that the socialist agenda the Democratic leadership treated for years as an electoral burden became the route to victory this time. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed beat Republican Mike Rogers by about 7 points on promises of government health insurance for all (Medicare for All) and taxes on the rich, even though AIPAC money was spent against him. In Maine, Troy Jackson, a logger turned politician, unseated Susan Collins.

In Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton by 12 points and became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a Senate seat there. The writer accepts that Talarico calls himself a capitalist, but says his campaign used the class language of 'top versus bottom'. Of the 21 candidates backed by Bernie Sanders, 17 won, and at least seven members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) will reach Congress.

Further down the ballot the picture is even clearer. The DSA won 130 contests and lost 42. Washington DC got its first socialist mayor in Janeese Lewis George, Florida elected a socialist legislator for the first time in a hundred years, and Missouri's voters rejected an abortion ban. Measures to restrict data centres passed almost everywhere.

The writer concludes that slogans like relief from rising prices and 'the fight against oligarchy' are no longer fringe ideas. He says this also opens the way for a left-wing presidential candidate in 2028, and that Democratic voters will no longer have to choose between heart and head.
nazar: This result overturns the old lesson that elections are won only by taking 'the middle road'. When candidates speak plainly about jobs, health care and prices and take on billionaires' money, people come along. The lesson for India's Opposition is the same: turning anger into votes needs concrete economic promises and grassroots organisation, not just anti-government noise.
sawal: After this win, will the Democratic leadership make room for this left wave?
ref: Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)
The largest socialist organisation in the US, whose members often run for office on the Democratic Party ticket.
Medicare for All
A proposal to give every American citizen health insurance at government expense, made popular by Bernie Sanders.

h: An apology from Britain is not enough; it must pay the debt of slavery
dek: Verene Shepherd, vice-chair of the CARICOM Reparations Commission, says Prime Minister Andy Burnham's offer of an apology is welcome, but debt relief cannot be made a substitute for reparations.
body: Reports say British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is ready to make a formal apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic trafficking and enslavement of Africans. Verene Shepherd, vice-chair of the reparations commission of CARICOM, the organisation of Caribbean countries, calls this a good start, but warns that the apology must be followed by real reparations, and that the path Burnham has suggested, easier terms for repaying debt, is no substitute.

The writer reminds us that Britain has so far only expressed 'deep regret' and has never apologised. In 2015 David Cameron rejected the demand for reparations and announced 25 million pounds to build a prison in Jamaica, so that Jamaican prisoners held in British jails could be sent back. She suspects this latest offer of an apology came under pressure from the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and the public protests there.

She says a true apology means accepting responsibility, promising never to repeat the wrong, and committing to repair the harm done to the descendants of the victims. It also means accepting that today's racial and economic inequality has its roots in that history.

She cites the Caribbean economist Sir Arthur Lewis, who wrote in 1939 that more than two hundred years of unpaid labour made Britain rich and that this 'black debt' is still owed. The writer also rejects Burnham's talk of a 'complex history': there is nothing complex about paying for the crime of slavery. She also says the credit for ending slavery goes not to Britain but to those who rebelled, such as Jamaica's Chief Tacky and the revolutionaries of Haiti.
Her demand is clear: debt cancellation based on the legacy of colonialism, cash reparations and serious talks on this. Britain should apologise and pay its debt.
nazar: India too suffered the plunder of the same empire, so this debate is ours as well. The language of apology often seems easy because it costs nothing. In our view the Caribbean countries are right to insist that history be settled not with words but with the return of resources, and the countries of the Global South should stand by one another in this demand.
sawal: Whose burden does an apology without reparations lighten?
ref: CARICOM
The joint organisation of Caribbean countries, whose reparations commission seeks redress from European countries for slavery and colonialism.
Ten-point plan
CARICOM's plan listing its reparations demands, such as a formal apology, debt cancellation, and investment in health and education.

h: In Sudan's war, no girl stands outside politics
dek: Sudanese activist Doha Ali uses her own life to show that this war is not just a civil war, nor just a humanitarian crisis, but a fight fed by weapons, money and Europe's migration deals.
body: At fifteen, before she went to university, Doha Ali's parents talked to her about politics. Her father said it was the art of achieving the possible; her mother said stay away from it, speaking out can get you hurt. Doha took her mother's words to heart. On campus, students avoided the 'political corners'.

The 2019 revolution brought that wall down. Politics left the home and came into cafes, buses and lanes, and neighbourhoods became places of organising and caring for one another. The writer says people organising themselves was a bigger threat to those in power than protest itself. Resistance did not stop even after the 2021 coup, and in April 2023 war broke out.

She asks how a militia became strong enough to fight the national army. The answer lies in the era of Omar al-Bashir, when the Janjaweed who fought in Darfur later became the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Then there is Europe's role: under the 2014 'Khartoum Process', money went into border management in Sudan to stop migration, and the RSF was deployed on the borders. The European Union says it did not fund the RSF directly, and the writer does not claim it did, but she says such cooperation gave tainted institutions legitimacy.

She crossed checkpoints of both the army and the RSF to reach Egypt, where she had to queue from four in the morning every day for a week for residence papers. There she understood that policies which push borders outward and treat migrants as a security problem were shaping not only the lives of those heading to Europe, but her own life too.

The writer says calling this a 'civil war' makes it an internal matter, and calling it 'the biggest humanitarian crisis' keeps attention on relief and away from the causes. It is also a proxy war, run by regional and international powers for their own interests.
nazar: A year after the destruction of El Fasher, the world still sees Sudan through the lens of relief supplies. Doha Ali's point matters: until those who supply the war with weapons and money are named, aid is only a bandage on the wound. And a society that 'protects' its daughters by frightening them away from politics in fact shuts them out of the very decisions that end up shaping their lives.
sawal: Whose hand do border-guarding contracts strengthen?
ref: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
A paramilitary force formed out of Darfur's Janjaweed militia, which has been at war with the Sudanese army since April 2023.
Khartoum Process
Talks between European and African countries begun in 2014, aimed at stopping migration from the Horn of Africa towards Europe.

h: Delhi's smoke has reached Goa, and nobody is in charge of the air
dek: Journalist Karanjeet Kaur says smaller cities are going Delhi's way too, because no single office is answerable for keeping a city's air clean.
body: After the pandemic, many Delhi families and professionals moved to Goa in search of clean air. The writer says that now the AQI there has touched 190 in some areas. Last December Panaji's average PM2.5 was 88 micrograms, 18 times the World Health Organization's limit. In Porvorim, breathing illnesses rose while an elevated road was being built.

This is not a one-off. Last year the world's most polluted city turned out to be Loni in Ghaziabad, and before that Byrnihat, an industrial town on the Assam-Meghalaya border. In Goa, a 2018 study found that more than 30 per cent of emissions come from transport and about 30 per cent from road dust and construction. The state has 13.5 lakh vehicles for about 15.9 lakh people, because public transport cannot be relied on. Mining and garbage burnt at night make things worse.
A WRI India study found that garbage burning triples in winter, and mostly in poor settlements, at exactly the hours when children and old people are outdoors.

The real problem is money and accountability. A Janaagraha report shows that of the National Clean Air Programme's 7,600 crore rupees, about two-thirds was spent on road dust, and less than one per cent on industry and household fuel. Of the 69 cities with data, only 10 met their target and the air got worse in 31. City bodies control the roads, not the factories or the vehicles, and the pollution job is often handed to some officer with no technical knowledge.

The suggestion is that every city should have a clean air cell of five to seven experts, and proper ways to measure. Waste management in Pune and Panaji shows that smaller cities can try new methods. Otherwise every place will end up like Delhi: an air purifier in every room, and looking away from everything else.
nazar: Homes that can buy an air purifier somehow escape; the smoke is thickest in the settlements where garbage is never collected. Until responsibility for the air is written on paper against someone's name, money will keep flowing into sprinkling water, and every winter new cities will join this list.
sawal: When a city's air has no owner, who will answer for it?
ref: PM2.5
Particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres floating in the air, which reach the lungs and blood and raise the risk of heart and breathing diseases.
National Clean Air Programme
A central government scheme launched in 2019, aiming to cut particulate pollution by 40 per cent in 130 polluted cities.

h: Peace in Manipur cannot be imposed from above; it must grow from within
dek: Bodoland leader and Rajya Sabha MP Pramod Boro says Manipur's wounds will heal not through security forces but through dialogue and patience between communities.
body: Pramod Boro, Rajya Sabha MP from Assam and president of the United People's Party Liberal, went to Imphal last week, his first visit since the violence began in May 2023. He met the Governor and the Chief Minister. The writer accepts that some people were suspicious of his visit, and calls this natural given the present lack of trust.

The ground for this visit was laid at the Northeast peace dialogue held at Tezpur University in October. The Tezpur Declaration, issued on 3 October, called for restoring trust in public institutions, a peace plan for the whole region, and peace education in schools.

The writer puts forward the experience of Bodoland, where after four decades of conflict more than 26 communities now live together across five districts. But he says clearly that this model will not fit Manipur as it is. Every conflict has its own history, so the initiative must come from Manipur's own communities. At the dialogue, people from all three major communities of Manipur also stressed a long, citizen-led effort.

In the writer's eyes Manipur is a human tragedy: lives lost, families uprooted, and children growing up seeing their neighbours as enemies. The habit of blaming a whole community hollows out our humanity. So along with security, there must be work on dialogue, education and healing minds. He sees the Northeast's traditions of farming together and celebrating festivals together as a store of trust.

His team calls itself a non-governmental citizens' initiative that will offer a platform for dialogue, counter rumours, and run sports, cultural and youth exchange programmes. The writer accepts that reconciliation will be slow, because grief does not pass quickly, trust does not come by order, and declarations of goodwill cannot take the place of justice.
nazar: For a politician to accept that trust does not come by order and that declarations do not replace justice is significant in itself. But for families forced to leave their homes, peace means going home, accountability and equal protection. A citizens' initiative will last only if governments also deliver their share of justice; otherwise peace talks will end up as a file of declarations.
sawal: How will a child who grew up seeing a neighbour as an enemy find the way back?
ref: Tezpur Declaration
The joint statement of the Northeast peace dialogue held at Tezpur University on 3 October 2026, calling for a regional peace plan and peace education.
Bodoland Territorial Region
An autonomous area of five Bodo-majority districts in Assam, formed after a long armed conflict and a series of accords.
photo_note: Kabir at the loom, a Mughal painting

h: Nepal: a government that promised transparency sent police into newsrooms
dek: The Kathmandu Post's editorial says plainclothes police picking up journalists from newsrooms shows that those in power are growing tired of questions.
body: On Friday, police in plain clothes entered several newsrooms in Kathmandu and detained reporters. They were released later, but the paper's editorial says the journalists became the news while doing their job. The paper sees this as an attempt to intimidate the media and stop unwelcome information from reaching the public.

What stings most is that this government rode in on the wave of the Gen Z movement, which raised the banner of transparency and accountability, and it has been in power for only seven months. The Prime Minister's secretariat says neither the Prime Minister nor his office knew of the arrests in advance. The paper asks: if that is true, it is a serious failure of executive oversight, and it needs explaining.

The editorial reminds readers that Nepal's Constitution treats full press freedom as a fundamental right: censoring news before publication, shutting a paper over its content or cancelling its registration are all barred. These are not favours from the government but constitutional guarantees. On 19 January 2005, King Gyanendra took direct rule and placed army officers in newsrooms. The press did not bow, that regime ended in 15 months, and later the monarchy itself was gone.

The paper accepts that the media has flaws, but says arrest is not the cure. Anyone unhappy with a story can go to the Press Council Nepal. The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party has been asked to answer, because this is not the first case: in July suspicious vehicles were seen parked outside media offices, and in August journalist Kishor Shrestha was arrested over a story. The demand is that the government apologise, explain the reason for the action and act against those responsible.
nazar: Even governments that come in on the slogan of change start to see questioners as a nuisance once they gain power; this lesson is not Nepal's alone. In India too, raids on journalists' homes and offices and their arrests no longer shock, and that is the most dangerous part. The Kathmandu Post's point is just as true for us: press freedom is not a gift from the government but a right given by the Constitution.
sawal: Why did a government born of a movement panic at questions so soon?
ref: Gen Z movement
The youth movement in Nepal that removed the old government over corruption and accountability, and opened the way for the new one.
Press Council Nepal
Nepal's statutory body that oversees the code of ethics for journalism and hears complaints about news reports.

h: An unsigned notice, and the police go after digital rights groups
dek: Delhi Police asked X to take down the entire accounts of the Internet Freedom Foundation and SFLC, on the strength of a notice in the RSS's name whose authenticity people from the Sangh itself have questioned.
body: On 29 October the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), the Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC) and 'Geo Blocked in India', an X account that keeps track of blocking orders, received a legal notice in the name of the RSS. It carried no one's name, only the words 'authorised signatory'. It demanded that they stop opposing government blocking orders and stop documenting blocked content, and confirm this within a week. Several office-bearers of the Sangh said on X that the notice was not genuine.

IFF replied the next day, asked the Sangh whether it had sent the notice, and made both documents public. The same day the Special Commissioner (Crime) of Delhi Police sent X a report of 'unlawful content'. It alleged defamation, but the box for a court order was empty. A later report added 37 posts and the entire accounts of all three organisations, along with posts by 16 other people who had commented on the notice, among them The Wire's editor Seema Chishti and Congress MP Nasir Hussain.

A second notice, which came on 1 November, said the matter had been handed over to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad. There are also reports of similar requests from the Uttar Pradesh and Telangana police.

IFF says defamation is not a police matter at all, that a court cannot take it up without a complaint from the aggrieved party, and that the police have become the enforcement agency for a private notice. The organisation has said it will go to court if the reports are not withdrawn.
nazar: Trying to get entire accounts removed without a court order, to silence the very groups that keep a record of censorship, shows how unchecked the power to block has become in India. There is also the question of why the police moved so fast on an unsigned piece of paper, when complaints from ordinary people lie untouched for months.
sawal: On whose behalf were the police speaking when they acted on an unsigned notice?
ref: Geo-blocking
Making a post or account invisible in just one country, while it stays visible in the rest of the world.
Internet Freedom Foundation
A Delhi-based organisation that argues in courts and in policy on issues like online expression, privacy and internet shutdowns.

h: The right to protest versus the right to trade: a new debate in the courts
dek: On traders' plea to ban protests in Delhi, the Supreme Court said both protest and livelihood are fundamental rights, while the Kerala High Court said satyagraha has no place in a democracy.
body: On Wednesday a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana heard a public interest litigation by traders who want every kind of protest in the capital banned for two months. Their association, represented by Mukul Rohatgi, is seeking compensation of Rs 1,000 crore for alleged losses caused by protests of the Cockroach Janata Party and the INDIA alliance.

The bench said the right to protest collides with the right to trade and practise a profession, and asked what would happen to daily wage workers. According to the Chief Justice, a place should be fixed where livelihoods are not hurt, and no single group should occupy a spot indefinitely. The court asked the petitioners to make the protest organisers parties to the case. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta spoke of recovering damages from the organisers, while several lawyers, including Menaka Guruswamy, argued that protest is part of freedom of expression.

The background: before the 2 October protest against SIR and the Chief Election Commissioner, permission for Jantar Mantar was cancelled, about 4,000 personnel were deployed, metro stations were shut and several leaders were detained.

The same day a division bench of the Kerala High Court said that dharnas (sit-ins), hunger strikes and satyagraha have no place in a constitutional democracy, especially in educational institutions. On this ground it overturned a single-judge order that had allowed 16 suspended students of the Sanskrit university in Kalady to sit their exams.
nazar: In a country that won its freedom through sit-ins and satyagraha, it is worrying to see courts weigh protest in a ledger of losses. Protest is bound to cause inconvenience; that is its purpose. If the fear of damages hangs over every protest, the first to fall silent will be those who have no platform but the street.
sawal: If a sit-in is 'anarchy', where are the weak to make themselves heard?
ref: Public interest litigation
A petition filed in court on a larger public question rather than a personal interest.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's fresh check of the voter rolls, in which voters are having to prove their eligibility all over again.

h: Siang dam: arrests, internet shutdowns and Rs 10.91 crore for PR
dek: Amid protests in Arunachal against an 11,200 megawatt project, Adivasi (indigenous) protesters face a harsh law, journalists' pages are shut down, and a Mumbai PR firm is hired to build support for the dam.
body: The movement in Arunachal against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project turned violent on 23 October after a 12-hour bandh (shutdown), when the NHPC office in Pasighat, a police station, and the homes of two MLAs and the state BJP president were set on fire. After this 69 people were arrested and about 55 cases are reported to have been filed. Since 9 October at least 10 protesters have been held under the state's own law on preventing unlawful activities.

According to independent fact-finding reports, the dam will submerge about 27 villages and displace nearly one and a half lakh people. Protester Tadak Nalo alleges that many of the consent letters the government cites are fake.

The internet was shut in Upper Siang until 2 November. Facebook accounts of protesters, journalists and local news pages were restricted or shut down. Police sought search warrants against Tongam Rina, deputy editor of the Arunachal Times, her lawyer and two activists.

Meanwhile NHPC has given Mumbai's Concept Public Relations a Rs 10.91 crore contract to build support for the project. Actor Taba Rima alleges that PR firms offered creators money for pro-dam content. Posts on social media calling the protesters China's pawns were also found, though a direct link between them and the PR contract is not proven. This investigation was originally done by Alt News.
nazar: The Adi community is asking questions about its land and its river, and in reply it gets a harsh law, internet shutdowns and paid propaganda. The violence must be condemned. But if consent really exists, why does proving it require shutting down journalists' pages?
sawal: Will a PR firm decide the consent of the villages along the river?
ref: NHPC
The central government's hydropower company, which builds large dams and power projects across the country.
Adi community
The main Adivasi community of Arunachal's Siang region, whose life and traditions are bound up with the river.

h: A third child, and she lost her post: Supreme Court questions the two-child rule
dek: The court said that in a time of falling fertility, two-child laws that disqualify people from local elections have become meaningless, and sent the matter to a larger bench.
body: Mangala Bhimrao, who was sarpanch (village head) of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra, was removed from her post after the birth of her third child. Since 2000 the Maharashtra Gram Panchayat Act has had a condition that people with more than two children cannot stay in the panchayat. Her appeal was dismissed, and in August 2025 the Bombay High Court also upheld the disqualification.

A bench of Justice P.S. Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe set aside her disqualification. The court said such laws shut a section of citizens out of political representation for a reason that has nothing to do with their ability to hold office, and force people to choose between children and democratic participation. The court linked this to reproductive freedom under Article 21.

The bench recalled that in 2003, when a similar Haryana law was upheld, the country's total fertility rate was 3. It is now 1.9, below the replacement rate of 2.1. This brings the risk of an ageing population, and China's example shows that such a decline is not easy to reverse. The matter has been sent to a larger bench to reconsider the 2003 judgment.
According to a list prepared by amicus curiae Rukmini Bobde, the rule is still in force in Assam, Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Uttarakhand.
nazar: The two-child rule hit hardest the women, Dalits and poor people who reached power for the first time through the panchayat, and who often do not even have full control over the decision to have children. These laws, built on a fear of population, no longer stand up even to the numbers. Why the delay in ending them?
sawal: How did counting children become a measure of a leader's ability?
ref: Total fertility rate
An estimate of how many children a woman gives birth to, on average, in her lifetime. At 2.1 the population stays stable.
Amicus curiae
Friend of the court: a lawyer the court appoints to give neutral advice in a case.

h: Names cut in SIR: fill Form 6, no fear of prosecution
dek: The Election Commission has assured that voters who were already registered will not face a false statement case just for filling Form 6, while the opposition called it a play on words.
body: Many people whose names are missing from the draft rolls of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) had been hesitating to fill Form 6. The reason: the form requires a declaration that the name is being added for the first time, and people who have voted for years feared this would be treated as a false statement.

On Tuesday the Commission wrote to the chief electoral officers of all states that no action would be taken against such voters under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, merely on the ground that they were registered before. The condition is that the person is not registered on the roll of another constituency. The Commission cited a 14 October ruling of the Delhi High Court and asked officers to publicise this clarification in local languages too.
Congress leader Jairam Ramesh called it a play on words that clears up nothing, and said SIR was designed precisely to keep people out. MP Sasikanth Senthil also criticised it.

The report recalls that within the Commission itself, Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu had objected in May to adding this declaration to Form 6, saying the power to change the rules lies with the central government. In August Sandhu even called the change unauthorised and illegal.
nazar: A voter who has voted for decades having to prove his loyalty by filling a first-time form is a system turned upside down. A letter may ease the fear, but until the wording of the form changes, the burden stays on the person whose name was cut.
sawal: Why should a voter of many years fill a 'first-time' form?
ref: Form 6
The application to add a new name to the voter roll, usually filled on turning 18 or on changing address.
Section 31
A provision of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, under which a false statement related to the voter roll can bring a sentence of up to one year.

h: Sudan: the fighting has paused, but factories lie in ruins and workers have no jobs
dek: A year after the army retook Khartoum, about 1,800 industrial units remain wrecked, and without power, capital and roads, industry cannot get back on its feet.
body: The war that broke out in April 2023 between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces brought thousands of businesses across the country to a halt. The capital, Khartoum, was the biggest battlefield. According to the industry ministry, about 1,800 industrial units were damaged and 650 were completely destroyed. The army took the city back last year, but industry has still not recovered.

Mansour Gaili, who runs a sweets factory, is working at 40 per cent of his old capacity and puts his losses on machines, spare parts and the building at about one million dollars. Sara Alfatih Khalil, who runs a sesame oil company, had 300 workers before the war. Her warehouses were looted and the factory is still shut. She says fewer than ten per cent of the factories in this sector are running.

Power shortages, broken roads, costly imports, scattered supply chains and a lack of capital are all standing in the way. Raw materials that were once found inside the country now have to be imported. There are few local goods in the market and prices change every day. Mohammed Haj, who lost his job when the war began, has still not found other work.

In August the ministry set up a committee to assess factories and offer incentives, but owners say they need real financial help, not promises. Economist Mohamed Alnayer suggests spreading industry across the whole country, beyond the capital.
nazar: War news stops at the death count, but the long damage that follows shows up in jobs and in everyday prices. The workers whose earnings turned to ash along with the factories are never mentioned in any ceasefire deal, and if rebuilding is limited to incentives for owners, they will be left behind again.
sawal: Who counts the cost of war from the worker's pocket?
ref: Rapid Support Forces
Sudan's paramilitary force, which grew out of Darfur's Janjaweed militia and has been fighting the army since 2023.
Khartoum
Sudan's capital, a city at the meeting point of two branches of the Nile.

h: Why was Alan Turing dragged in again to defend Alokdhanva?
dek: Aditya Shukla says that calling Turing's homosexuality a perversion while defending the poet Alokdhanva kills the mathematician a second time, and is also an attempt to silence women's complaints.
body: This piece by Aditya Shukla, published on Sammukh, is a response to a fresh controversy. A woman writer objected on social media to the behaviour of the Hindi poet Alokdhanva. According to the author, the allegations include calling women again and again late at night, improper remarks disguised as praise, obscene material on his wall, and posting pictures of women without permission. Defending the poet, the critic Prem Kumar Mani compared him to Alan Turing.

Shukla first reminds us who Turing was: one of the people who laid the foundations of modern computer science, whose team broke the German Enigma code in the Second World War. The same Britain punished him for the 'crime' of being homosexual, had him chemically castrated with drugs and declared him a security risk. In 1954 he was found dead in his room. The official record called it suicide, but according to the author it was in fact a killing by the state. At the start he also cites a gay character from a Sartre novel, to show how heavy social pressure can be even when something is not a crime.
According to the author, Mani not only misspelled Turing's name but called his sexuality a sexual perversion. Shukla sees this as the thinking of 1954, which humiliates Turing once again.

His second argument is that the two cases have nothing in common. Turing was crushed by the state; Alokdhanva has lost no rights, and he is a famous and respected poet. Shukla calls the defences offered by Mamta Kalia and Kumar Ambuj either naive or clever, and says that if the poet is ill, his well-wishers should get him treated instead of attacking his critics.
Whatever someone puts on his own wall, the author says, no one has the right to cross a woman's personal boundaries. The essay asks the Hindi literary community which side of justice it stands on.
nazar: In the world of Hindi literature, deference to the 'great writer' often weighs more than the woman who complains. This piece matters because it stops two separate struggles, the dignity of queer people and the safety of women, from being used against each other.
In our view the allegations should be investigated and there should be accountability, but defaming another person on the margins in the name of a defence is never acceptable.
sawal: How did a poet's stature become bigger than hearing a complaint?
ref: Alan Turing
British mathematician (1912-1954), regarded as the father of computer science. He was punished for homosexuality and received a posthumous royal pardon in 2013.
Alokdhanva
A well-known Hindi poet, known for the collection 'Duniya Roz Banti Hai' (The world is made every day) and poems like 'Bhagi Hui Ladkiyan' (Girls who ran away).
photo_note: The End of the Journey, Abanindranath Tagore

h: He found his old friend, but the friend remembered nothing
dek: In Ratan Chand 'Ratnesh''s story, a retired man recognises a friend from thirty-five years ago, but the friend does not recognise him, and the address he gives turns out to be wrong.
body: Ratan Chand 'Ratnesh''s story 'Khoye Hue Log' (Lost people), published on Sammukh, is set in a planned city whose sectors are known by numbers and look alike. The narrator, Chandan, has retired from a government job and is out on a scooter with his wife.

One evening he sees Vinod feeding stray dogs by the roadside. Vinod was once his neighbour and chess partner, then a mechanic with Punjab Roadways. The surprise is that thirty-five years later Vinod looks just the same. Chandan lists old memories: evenings spent together, a book of Mukesh's songs that Vinod took and never returned, news of a job that he had passed on. Vinod listens politely but remembers nothing. All he admits is that he is retired, alone and childless, and he gives his house number.

Later, when the couple reach that address, the man who opens the door says no one by that name lives there. In the end it turns out they were standing in the wrong sector. The story ends right there, with no resolution, in tiredness and confusion.

The story's strength lies in its simplicity. Most of it moves through dialogue, and the details are everyday ones: house numbers, sectors, the scooter stopping. Among them a strange unease grows: was this meeting real, was someone deliberately avoiding him, or is memory itself playing tricks?
The question left for the reader is how much of our identity rests on the people who remember us.
nazar: This is often what old age looks like in India's newly built cities: identical houses, scattered neighbours, and friendships that survive only as one person's memory. The story touches that loneliness without making any noise.
We liked this story because it is in no hurry to solve its mystery, and makes the incompleteness itself its answer.
sawal: What if the one we remember has forgotten us?
ref: Planned city
A city built to a map drawn up in advance, like Chandigarh, where areas are divided into numbered sectors.
Mukesh
A famous playback singer of Hindi films (1923-1976), whose songs full of sorrow are part of the memories of a whole generation.

h: Feminism in DU seminars, 'bro code' at the dhaba
dek: Shivani alleges that beneath Delhi University's progressive image, caste, feudal thinking and contempt for women survive unchanged, and tomorrow these same students will become professors.
body: In Hindwi's Bela column, Shivani, who describes herself as an independent observer of campus life, begins with a picture of Delhi University's North Campus: the steps of the Arts Faculty, the tea stalls, Faiz's poems, badges, debates on patriarchy and caste. From the outside the place looks like a hub of revolution and modernity.

Her claim is that this image is a curtain. According to the writer, the same students who speak loudly about Marx and Ambedkar in class go back to caste, gotra (clan lineage) and family honour as soon as marriage comes up. She describes a pattern: a partner from a small town or a non-upper-caste background puts her time and trust into studies and emotional support, and is dropped the moment the question of social approval arises.

The writer says she has heard such stories in hostels and faculties from girls of different states and classes. Those who read papers on feminism and subaltern studies in seminars, and who prepare for JRF and PhD, comment at dhabas (roadside eateries) on girls' clothes and the way they walk. She regards the silence of the academic world as complicity.

She makes clear that her target is not all boys but a pack mentality, and that there are sensitive students on campus too. Her biggest worry is how these same people, once they become professors, will look at their women students.

Finally she asks vice-chancellors and senior teachers when basic ethics and respect for women will be taught alongside theory. The essay gives no names or figures; it is a critique based on personal observation and testimonies she has heard.
nazar: On India's campuses, sexual harassment complaint committees often exist only on paper, and talk of caste goes quiet at the threshold of marriage. This piece reminds us that speaking a progressive language and living in a progressive way are two different things.
In our view such allegations will have an effect only when institutions offer a reliable way to record testimony; otherwise this anger too will remain just another debate at the tea stall.
sawal: Whom does the one who teaches equality in seminars choose at home?
ref: Subaltern studies
A school that reads history and society from the point of view of people on the margins, peasants, Dalits and Adivasis, associated with Ranajit Guha in the 1980s.
JRF
Junior Research Fellowship, a research scholarship awarded through UGC-NET, often seen as the first step towards an academic job.

h: Popular fiction: the first rung of the ladder, not the destination
dek: Kushagra Mishra asks what standing the popular novels dismissed as pulp really have, and finds the answer in where the reader stands.
body: This essay by Kushagra Mishra, published on Hindwi's 'Bela', does not move in a straight line. The writer says at the start that he will make his point in a roundabout way, moving from small experiences to large conclusions, as was Francis Bacon's method.

Then he goes back to 2020, the year of Covid, when he finished his intermediate (school-leaving) exams. According to him, ordinary life is shaped by the narrow thinking inherited from patriarchy, caste and relationships called 'normal', and society is a slaughterhouse where people think themselves content even as they are wounded.

The writer says that fleeing this circle to the forest is no answer, because society also sits inside the mind. The way out is Montaigne's 'back room', a corner of solitude within oneself. But solitude brings unease, which, drawing on Kierkegaard, he calls the dizziness of freedom: the lone person stands at the edge of the abyss of his own autonomy and chooses whether to leap or to put on a comfortable mask.

This is where popular fiction comes in. The writer sees it as the first rung on the ladder of awakening, easy to enter, and able to lead to a new awareness, though it guarantees no fixed destination. If a new reader asks whether to read Kafka or Pessoa, the answer depends on where that reader stands. Heavy books read too early can have the opposite effect.

He also holds that moving forward does not happen by itself. Many devotees never get from saguna worship (worship of God with form) to nirguna reflection (on God without form), yet worship loses none of its worth; and in Patanjali's yoga you cannot skip yama (the first ethical step) and go straight to samadhi. The essay ends with a sher (couplet) which says that once the first step is taken, the darkness ahead is not there to frighten you.
nazar: The Hindi literary world has often looked down on popular novels, even though crores of readers learned to read with them. This essay gently breaks that arrogance and places the reader on a journey rather than in the dock.
In our view the matter should not stop here: if popular fiction is the first rung, then libraries, cheap books and schools have a duty to keep the next rung within reach too.
sawal: Which book started your reading habit?
ref: Popular fiction
Detective, romantic or thriller novels written for ordinary readers, often called 'lugdi' (pulp) literature in Hindi.
Montaigne
Sixteenth-century French writer who shaped the essay form and spoke of keeping a private corner within oneself.
Kierkegaard
Nineteenth-century Danish philosopher who saw anxiety as an experience bound up with freedom.

h: Death in an officer's poems, as the ego dissolves
dek: Two poems by Madhya Pradesh IAS officer Sukhvir Singh see death not as something to fear but as the moment a burden is set down.
body: Shabdankan has published two poems by Sukhvir Singh. He is a senior IAS officer of the Madhya Pradesh cadre and is currently principal secretary in the public works department and the medical education department. According to the introduction by editor Bharat Tiwari, his poetry weaves together love, a philosophy of life and worldly truth.

The first poem is in free verse and flows almost like prose. In it death comes not as a frightening guest but as a familiar companion. At its centre is the relief that there will be no more need to prove oneself, that social identities and roles will fall away, and that perhaps it will turn out the life one held on to so tightly was an illusion. Its images are forgotten forest paths, a hand someone held, the dust gathered over many lifetimes, and questions burning like lamps.

The second poem is rhymed and tightly bound. Here the heart is like a bottomless well, at whose bottom lies a sleeping seed of life. Fear and compassion walk side by side: a fierce flame, a guard standing at the threshold, and closed eyes that begin to look within.
The last turn of this poem is the most interesting. The heart the poet always thought was his own is found resting on someone else's open palm. That is, the 'I' ends not in some void but in love.
On this basis Bharat Tiwari says that in these poems death is not an ending but the dissolving of the ego, and that in the end these are love poems.
nazar: It is no small thing that a man who lives every day in a world of files, posts and orders writes poetry longing for release from that very identity. This inner voice of people in the corridors of power is rarely heard.
In our view the real test of such poetry will come when this humility reaches the office desk too, where the ordinary person still stands in a queue to prove himself.
sawal: How does a man in a seat of power write about freedom from identity?
ref: Shabdankan
An online Hindi literary magazine edited by Bharat Tiwari.
Free verse
Poetry that is not bound by fixed metre, rhythm or rhyme.

h: When JNU wrote love letters to Jamia
dek: In this piece by Ashish Kumar Shah, JNU is a lover and Jamia his beloved, and the story of an unfinished love unfolds over six letters.
body: Published in the 'Patra' (Letters) series on Hindwi's 'Bela', this piece is a sequence of six letters. The writer is JNU, who is in love with Jamia Millia Islamia, and every letter ends with 'Yours, JNU'. The campus here is not just a backdrop; it becomes the lover's body and temperament.

The first letter recalls a first meeting on a January evening, sitting by a bonfire, and the complaint that JNU has no lake, so he sees a lake in her eyes. It also gives the reason for writing letters in the age of social media. Alongside comes a full picture of the campus: bougainvillea in March, Holi and Ramzan, the ring road, rocks, peacocks and nilgai (blue bulls), a saved seat in the library, seminars, protests against the Dean of Students, and the buzz of student union elections.

In the letters that follow, the tone changes. No reply comes, the phone is switched off, and the lover wonders whether this relationship was one-sided all along. He also admits his own failings: comparing her with an old girlfriend, not being able to say his love in words, and trusting that the other person would read feelings from actions.

In between there is a journey, to an international seminar in Chidambaram and a tour of Tamil Nadu, bringing in the sea, Annamalai University and the warmth of a new friend, Gautam. The longing for a world free of the pressures of caste, religion and society is also recorded here.

The last letter reveals that the old girlfriend has come back and the lover has decided to give her another chance. In the middle of a trip around Delhi, he tells Jamia that he cannot return now, but he will not forget either.
nazar: Turning two universities into lover and beloved is no small thing at a time when both campuses are often seen only in the language of suspicion, police and headlines. This piece shows them again as places of living people who read and love.

In our view its weakness is that the metaphor goes slack in many places and the letters turn into a private diary. Even so, the small campus things it records, the canteen, the library, the protests, remind us of a shared heritage that must be kept alive.
sawal: Can calling a campus your beloved be a way of saving it?
ref: Jamia Millia Islamia
A central university in Delhi, founded in 1920 during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Epistolary form
A work told in the form of letters, where the story moves forward one letter after another.
photo_note: Sultan Suleiman hunting, a miniature from the Suleymanname
